Sample sizes are decent for Metaculus (thousands of forecasters, audited near-term calibration) and poor for the aggregate, which is an ensemble of five heterogeneous series rather than an independent sample. Class B is announcement-timing markets, which is closer to this question's actual resolution bar. The gap between Class A (about 30%) and Class B (about 50-55%) is mostly definitional. Metaculus requires robotic plus cognitive generality; Kalshi and Polymarket resolve on declarations. This question resolves on an announcement or on three researchers asserting achievement, so it sits nearer the Class B bar, which argues for a number above 32%. Two things cut the other way. First, the resolver requires a credible lab announcement, and the labs are actively de-emphasising the word: Altman calls the term 'hugely overloaded', which suppresses the announcement hazard rate independent of capability. A third weaker class is capability extrapolation: METR's time horizon doubling every 4-7 months, with the strongest agents at roughly 16-20 hours on the 50% horizon and METR explicitly cautioning that estimates above 16 hours are unreliable due to suite saturation. That trend is consistent with 2027-2030 arrival but the measurement instrument is degrading exactly where it matters. Limitations throughout: no consensus AGI definition, thin market volume, and heavy correlation between the aggregator's own inputs.

forecasts.base_rate: The reference class is professional-services sectors losing a third or more of revenue or employment inside roughly six years, with the loss primarily attributed to one technology by multiple credible analyses. That class is genuinely small. Travel agencies shed 40-50% of employment but over about fifteen years, and the causal agent was disintermediation of a transactional booking function, not the automation of judgement. Legal document review contracted sharply but was a discrete, commoditised task inside a much larger sector rather than a sector itself. Typesetting and photo processing collapsed faster, but both were physical-craft occupations with a single output that a machine reproduced exactly. Stenography, film processing and directory assistance round out the class. In each case the automated thing was the whole product. Economic consultancy fails that test structurally. What clients buy is a bundle: quantitative analysis, expert testimony admissible before a court or regulator, relationship capital with counsel and agencies, political and legal cover, insurable accountability, and a credential that survives cross-examination. AI compresses the analysis layer, which is real but is perhaps a third to a half of the delivered hours and a smaller share of the fee. The other layers are not merely unautomated but arguably become more valuable as machine-generated analysis proliferates, because signing your name to a number in front of a tribunal is a liability transfer that no model can perform. The 12 August 2026 Big Four hallucination story is a live demonstration of exactly that asymmetry. Against this, three adjustments push the base rate up. First, unlike prior technologies, AI attacks the pyramid economics that fund senior capacity: graduate intake cuts of 6-30% at the Big Four, McKinsey's 2026 BA class down ~20% versus 2024, BCG's 15% cut in entry-level consulting roles. Second, pricing is decoupling from hours, with over 30% of McKinsey's global fees now outcome-linked, which can compress sector revenue without any loss of client demand. Third, the May 2026 Anthropic and OpenAI PE-backed enterprise services ventures, roughly $1.5bn and $10bn respectively, are the first credible AI-native entrants targeting the $375bn management consulting pool. A further complication is definitional. Economic consultancy specifically is unusually insulated: it is litigation, regulatory and merger driven, and H1 2026 global M&A of $2.85tn (up 50%) is a bigger swing factor than AI in either direction. If the resolver reads 'economic consultancy' narrowly as CRA, NERA, Cornerstone, Brattle, Compass Lexecon and Frontier, current evidence points the wrong way entirely. If read broadly as advisory, the pyramid-erosion channel is more plausible. Synthesising: outside view of 5-12%, adjusted to 15-20% for the AI trajectory, entry-level compression and pricing deflation, then discounted for the demanding attribution bar ('primarily attributed to AI by 2+ credible analyses') which cyclical noise will make hard to clear cleanly by 2030. Central 17%.

forecasts.base_rate: The reference class is a governing party three years out from a required election, having changed leader mid-term, and currently level-pegging or narrowly ahead in a fragmented five-party system. Three anchors matter. First, incumbency and seat efficiency. Since 1945 the largest party at the previous election has been largest again at the following one in a clear majority of cases; governments usually lose vote share but first-past-the-post plus geographically efficient support cushions seat loss. Labour's 2024 coalition, even shrunken to the mid-20s, remains the most efficiently distributed in Great Britain, which is why seat models and MRPs keep projecting Labour largest on vote shares at or below Reform's. PLMR/Electoral Calculus has Labour largest on 217 seats at 22 percent while Reform on the same 22 percent takes 127. PollCheck's model has Labour largest on 268. This decoupling of votes and seats is the single most important structural fact in this question. Second, mid-term leadership changes. UK precedents are mixed but not disastrous: Major 1990, Brown 2007, Johnson 2019, Sunak 2022. Major and Johnson went on to win most seats; Brown and Sunak did not. That gives a rough base rate near 50 percent, though Major and Johnson benefited from calling early elections while the honeymoon lasted, which is a live option here given Burnham's +16 net approval. Third, poll-to-outcome mapping at three years out. Mid-term leads at T-36 months are weakly predictive; historic mean absolute error on vote share is large and lead reversals are common. Reform's own trajectory illustrates the volatility: from 31 percent in PLMR's January poll to 22-24 percent now, driven by the Harborne and Cottrell finance stories and by Restore Britain splitting the right. Right-of-centre fragmentation across Reform, Conservatives and Restore Britain is the mechanism most likely to deliver Labour a plurality of seats on a historically low plurality of votes. Against these, two base-rate drags. Governing parties polling in the mid-20s in mid-term usually go on to lose vote share further once a Budget imposes real costs, and 28 October is the first hard test. And prediction markets, which have decent calibration on UK seat questions, currently sit near 35-40 percent for Labour most seats, well below this forecast. Reconciling the structural seat-efficiency argument with the market price is the central open question and is why the interval stays wide.

forecasts.base_rate: Outside view remains the anchor. The broad reference class is major-power amphibious assault or sustained naval blockade against defended territory since 1945: a handful of cases in eighty years, implying an annual hazard in the low single digits. Applied to the 3.4 years remaining to 1 January 2030 that yields roughly 3 to 8 percent, before any adjustment for China-specific capability, intent and opportunity. The narrower and more informative class is Taiwan Strait coercion episodes since 1995. The 1995-96 missile crises, the August 2022 Pelosi encirclement, Joint Sword 2024A and 2024B, Strait Thunder 2025A and Justice Mission 2025 all involved declared closure areas, live fire and encirclement geometry, and none converted into a sustained blockade or an assault on Taiwan proper. That is now 0 for 7. Each episode has been designed to be reversible, time-boxed to days, and terminated on Beijing's own announcement. This is a strong signal that the PLA uses exercises as signalling instruments rather than as mobilisation cover, and it argues for a low conditional probability that any given escalation converts. Against that, the reference class is not static. The relevant hazard is shifting from invasion toward quarantine, which is a lower-threshold, law-enforcement-framed action. The CCG began patrols east of Taiwan in June 2026 and has rotated task groups (Daishan replaced by Xiushan on 4 July), converting a one-off assertion into a standing patrol calendar and prompting Bloomberg, Korea Times and others to describe it as a new normal. February 2026 CCG statements pledged normalisation of patrols and institutionalised control in sensitive maritime areas. The Guangdong MSA typhoon traffic-control order and the EEZ-jurisdiction framing around the Indonesia drill are consistent legal-precedent building. Note, however, that a quarantine of the CSIS or RAND type would only resolve this question YES if it lasted more than 72 hours and were characterised by two major agencies as a blockade. A short, law-enforcement-branded interdiction of a handful of vessels would probably not resolve YES. Capability trend is upward: the Type 076 Sichuan is expected to be delivered by end-2026, and the 2027 centenary readiness milestone falls inside the window. Restraint indicators remain strong: PLA monthly incursion volume has reverted to the pre-Lai baseline since the start of 2026, Beijing is prioritising the 28 November local elections and the 24 September Xi visit to Washington, and the US arms-sale pause since May 2026 gives Beijing a reason to protect the current trajectory. Blending the two classes and weighting the narrow one more heavily for the near term, then adding a modest premium for the 2027-2029 tail when capability, the political calendar and possible US distraction converge, supports a central around 7 percent. The distribution is right-skewed: most of the probability mass sits in 2028-2029, not in the next twelve months.

forecasts.base_rate: The structural base rate here is set by publication mechanics rather than by any historical frequency of low inflation. Only five reference months, July through November 2026, can be published before 1 January 2027, running from the 19 August release to the mid-December release. December 2026 CPI is published in mid-January 2027 and cannot count. So the question is really: does any one of five specific monthly prints, starting from a 2.6% June base, come in below 2.0%? Historically, UK CPI moves by roughly 0.1 to 0.3pp per month absent a policy or energy step-change. Month-on-month swings of 0.7pp or more happen almost exclusively when an administered price resets, most obviously the April Ofgem cap change or the October cap change, or when a VAT rate moves. Over the 2015-2025 sample, the unconditional share of months with CPI below 2.0% is around 45%, but that is dominated by the 2015-2021 low-inflation regime and by the mid-2024 window. Conditioning on the current regime is what matters. Conditioning first on the starting level, the historical probability that CPI drops 0.7pp or more within four months from a 2.6% base is roughly 15-20%, and almost all of those episodes involve a falling energy cap. Conditioning second on the direction of the energy step, the October cap is now forecast up 2.2-2.4% rather than down, and the year-ago comparison base for household energy is low, so October and November mechanically carry a positive energy contribution. That flips the sign of the only mechanism large enough to deliver the required drop. Conditioning third on the composition of the index, CPI services ran at 3.6% in June and all-goods at 1.7%. With services at roughly 45-50% of the basket, headline below 2.0% would require goods inflation near zero or negative while energy is rising, which is not a configuration seen outside of 2015-16 or 2020. Conditioning fourth on the forecaster distribution, no mainstream body has a sub-2% path for any month in 2026. BoE July MPR: 3.2% Q4. Deutsche Bank: peak 3.3-3.5% Q4. HM Treasury panel (17 June): 3.7% Q4. NIESR: 3.1% 2026 average. OBR pre-conflict: 2.3% annual. Every one of these is above 2.0% for the whole horizon. Combining these, the conditional base rate is in the 1-3% range, and the residual probability comes almost entirely from a single tail path: a rapid, verified Hormuz reopening in August collapsing Brent and NBP, combined with a large upstream forecast error, arriving in time to affect the October or November reference months. That path is now demonstrably narrowing.

forecasts.base_rate: The reference class here is not 'blockbusters that reach $1.5B' but 'already-recorded box office milestones that are subsequently unrecorded'. Once a film's cumulative worldwide gross is published by both Box Office Mojo and The Numbers, the number is monotonic in practice: theatrical grosses accumulate and are never reversed, because refunds, comp tickets and currency effects are handled inside the reported figures rather than by clawing back prior totals. Across the modern era of tracked releases there is no case of a major studio title's published worldwide cumulative being revised downward by anything close to double digits in percentage terms after the film crossed a round-number threshold. Typical revisions to worldwide totals fall in the 0.1%-2% band and arise from three sources: (a) the routine estimate-to-actual correction on weekend numbers, usually under 3% on a single frame and therefore well under 1% of a $1.7B cumulative; (b) currency retranslation of international grosses, which can shift a territory total by a few percent but almost never moves a global aggregate by more than 1%-2% and is as likely to move up as down; and (c) reclassification of re-releases, double bills or premium-format runs into or out of the main release group, which is material only for small titles. The largest genuinely contentious restatements in the historical record involve disputed reporting in individual territories, most notably China and India, where studio-reported and local-regulator figures have diverged. Even in the most-cited disputes the contested amount has been in the tens of millions on films grossing over a billion, i.e. low single-digit percentages. Brand New Day's China total of $132.9M on The Numbers (Deadline cites $186.7M cumulative, a discrepancy that itself reflects lagged territory reporting rather than dispute) is only about 8-11% of the worldwide total, so even total invalidation of the Chinese gross would leave the film comfortably above $1.5B. A second relevant reference class is source availability. Box Office Mojo and The Numbers have both operated continuously for over two decades; the base rate of either permanently removing a live blockbuster's page inside a four-and-a-half-month window is negligible, and the question resolves on either source, so both would have to fail simultaneously. Transient retrieval failures of the kind seen today are common and carry no informational content about the underlying record. Combining a downward-restatement hazard of well under 1 in 10,000 for a cut of the required 12%+ magnitude with a dual-source-failure hazard of similar order gives a residual failure probability comfortably below 0.1%, which is why the estimate sits at the 100 ceiling.

Also 12 August, Anthropic, Macquarie Asset Management and GIC announced Theseus Infrastructure, a purpose-built data-centre platform majority-funded by Macquarie and GIC with Anthropic absorbing consumer electricity price increases (Bloomberg 10 Aug, Macquarie release, DCD). On 10 August Riot Platforms disclosed a 20-year, 191 MW Rockdale lease that Bloomberg identifies as Anthropic, worth about $9.1bn base and up to $16.1bn with extensions. No named outlet published a fresh ARR print for either firm on 12 or 13 August. Fundamentals that firmed. TRIGGER CHECK. 1 (Anthropic public S-1 restates net below $47bn): DID NOT FIRE. No public S-1 on EDGAR from either firm as of 13 Aug; the gross-versus-net question remains open and only in SEC review. 2 (named outlet reports MoM decline, or combined below $70bn): DID NOT FIRE. Deceleration in growth rate is reported, but no decline and no sub-$70bn combined figure anywhere. 3 (OpenAI formally defers to 2027 AND Anthropic slips past Q4): DID NOT FIRE, and is now half-refuted - WSJ on 12 Aug has Anthropic aiming at September or early October. The tender completion is a weak deferral hint at most. 4 (qualifying Q4 print for both above $70bn): DID NOT FIRE, which is exactly why the estimate cannot go above 99. 5 (EDGAR monitoring): nothing public yet; OpenAI's prospectus is still expected mid-to-late August. The judgement: the bar is now cleared several times over on almost any accounting basis, including a punitive net restatement of Anthropic. The only live failure mode is a reporting vacuum, and the Anthropic roadshow plus OpenAI's expected prospectus both cut against it.
forecasts.base_rate: The reference class is 'threshold already crossed on current reported figures, with the question asking whether it stays crossed and gets documented.' Questions of this shape resolve YES at very high rates, typically 95-99%, because they require no new growth, only continuity plus publication. The residual failure modes are definitional rather than economic. A second reference class is revenue-trajectory persistence for hypergrowth private software companies over a four-to-five month horizon. Firms adding revenue at Anthropic's and OpenAI's observed rate have essentially never printed an absolute run-rate decline over a single quarter absent a discrete shock such as a product withdrawal, a major customer loss or a fraud restatement. Anthropic's own path (roughly $9bn end-2025, $14bn Feb, $19bn Mar, $30bn Apr, $47bn May disclosed) and OpenAI's ($25bn Feb, $33bn May, $41.3bn July on TickerTrends) both sit deep in the persistence regime. Even a hard stall at July levels leaves the combined figure at $115bn on tracker basis, or roughly $72bn using only the conservative company-confirmed anchors ($47bn Anthropic disclosed May, $25bn OpenAI confirmed). A third and more binding reference class is disclosure availability. For high-salience private companies under active IPO preparation, the probability that at least one of Bloomberg, The Information, FT or the company itself publishes a run-rate figure within any given quarter has historically been near-unity for both firms: Anthropic has had named-outlet run-rate prints in January, March, April and May 2026 alone, and OpenAI has had CFO-sourced disclosures repeatedly. Add a live S-1 process for both and the probability of a Q4-adjacent figure for each rises further, since a public prospectus forces audited quarterly revenue into the open. The accounting dispute deserves an explicit base-rate treatment. Forced gross-to-net restatements at IPO typically cut headline revenue by 20-40% where they occur, and they occur in perhaps a fifth to a third of contested cases. Applying a 40% haircut to a plausible Anthropic Q4 gross run-rate of $80-90bn still leaves $48-54bn, and OpenAI at $40-50bn takes the combined figure to $88-104bn. The threshold survives the worst plausible accounting outcome. Calibration anchor: for questions where the stated quantity already exceeds the bar by 40-60% with four months of tailwind remaining, and where the only genuine risk is a resolution-source technicality, 98-99% is the defensible band. Going to 99.5% or higher would require the qualifying Q4 print itself to be in hand.

forecasts.base_rate: The naive outside view is favourable. UK decade averages for annual real GDP growth were roughly 2.2% in the 1990s, 1.8% in the 2000s and 2.0% in the 2010s, with the 2020s running near 1.0% to date. Three of the last four decades cleared 1.5%, giving an unadjusted base rate around 60-75%. That reference class is badly contaminated. The pre-2008 decades were built on labour productivity growth of roughly 2% a year plus rapid labour force expansion from rising female participation and, later, EU accession migration. Neither driver is available for the 2030s. The 2010s figure of 2.0% is itself misleading, resting on a deep post-crisis output gap that mechanically flattered measured growth through recovery rather than trend. The forward decomposition is the better anchor. Potential growth equals trend productivity plus trend hours or labour supply. OBR's November 2025 assumption put underlying medium-term productivity growth at 1.0% a year, cut from 1.3%, and reporting ahead of the 28 October 2026 Budget points to a further 0.1-0.2pp reduction. The IMF's 2026 Article IV assessed UK potential growth at 1.4% and judged the economy to have grown at potential in 2025. On labour supply, ONS 2024-based projections have natural change turning negative from 2026, with net migration falling to about 138,000 in 2026 before stabilising near 230,000, implying working-age population growth decelerating toward 0.3-0.5% a year across the 2030s and lower still if participation keeps drifting down (economic inactivity has been rising since late 2025). Adding roughly 1.0-1.1% productivity to roughly 0.3-0.5% labour supply gives potential of about 1.3-1.6%, straddling the threshold with the central estimate marginally below it. That framing implies a probability somewhat below 50% before considering shocks. Shocks are asymmetric against the question. A decade average is dragged down far more by one recession year of -3% than it is lifted by a boom year of +3%, and the 2030s carry non-trivial odds of at least one recession, an energy or geopolitical disruption, a climate or water-security event, or a fiscal crisis given gilts near 5% and debt interest above £110bn. Reference-class forecasting of decade-ahead OECD growth also shows persistent forecaster optimism: official medium-term projections have systematically overshot realised outcomes since 2008. Against that, the genuine upside case is an AI-driven productivity acceleration arriving with a lag into the 2030s, which is precisely when a general purpose technology diffusion story would predict measured gains. UK 2030s growth also benefits if the current capital-deepening push, including the £9bn-a-year investment borrowing under discussion, actually raises the capital stock. Weighing a central potential estimate marginally under the bar, negatively skewed shock risk, and a fat but uncertain AI upside tail leaves the low-to-mid 30s as the defensible range.
